s01: Eight o'clock. The pills are on the table. And Ammi asks the hardest question in our house. Did I take my medicine already?
s02: Alarm apps only tell you when. For a person with memory loss, that is not enough. A reminder is not remembering. Mathaka answers whether you already took it, and it stops a second dose.
s03: Mathaka means memory, in Sinhala. It is one app, with two roles. A simple elder phone, which can be an old, cheap Android. And a family phone, for the son, the daughter, or the pharmacist we call the Memory Buddy.
s04: On Ammi's phone, it is simple. It is time for your morning medicine. She sees only the pills for now, as big pictures, with their purpose, never a drug name. She taps, I took it. The app asks once more, did you swallow the pills now? Then it writes it down.
s05: Later, she asks again. Did I take my medicine? The answer comes from the log, in the same calm words, every time. Yes, Ammi. You took your morning medicine at eight. And if she tries to take it twice, Mathaka gently tells her she already did. The double dose never happens.
s06: Everything is made for older eyes and hands. Sinhala, Tamil and English. Huge text, seven to one contrast, a high contrast theme, a real clock, and, say it again. No swipes. No double taps. A son can even record the reminders in his own voice.
s07: On the family phone, Nimal sees the day at a glance. Doses taken, the next one, missed doses, low stock, the clinic date, and a week of history. A fridge card prints every pill on paper, for the days the phone is off.
s08: Here is the breakthrough. Heavy AI, once. Light AI, every day. And no cloud, anywhere.
s09: Once, during setup, the family phone runs Gemma 3, an open vision model, right on the phone, with llama dot R N. It reads the prescription into rows, and reads the number printed on each pill. Every answer is forced into a JSON schema, checked, and retried once. And a person confirms every row, before it is used.
s10: Then each pill is measured, not guessed. You place it on a printed mat, with four markers. Plain TypeScript finds the markers, flattens the perspective, and turns pixels into millimetres. It balances the colour on a grey patch, cuts out the pill, and measures its size, shape, colour, two tone halves, and score line. Nineteen point two, by nine point two millimetres, in about two hundred milliseconds. The same code runs on the phone, in the browser, and in the tests.
s11: A second person must approve the whole setup. Then it travels as one file, by Bluetooth, a cable, or WhatsApp to yourself. Every part is checked with S H A two fifty six. The elder phone rejects a file that is broken, changed, older, or not approved.
s12: Some things need understanding, like what Ammi meant, in Singlish. For that, we tested Laya, an open decision model that can only pick from a short list. It cannot write a sentence. And no model ever writes words for Ammi. Every sentence she hears is a fixed template, filled with facts from her own log.
s13: When a dose is missed, the family knows. First over the home Wi-Fi, paired once with a QR code. If that fails, by plain SMS, with no internet at all. Anything not delivered is tried again, in the background.
s14: And there is an optional Arduino pill box. An E S P thirty two lights the slot that is due, and blinks gently when it is late. Pressing the lit slot means, I took it, through the same double dose guard. The box never decides. You can even try it in the Wokwi simulator.
s15: We measured it honestly, on frozen test sets. Forty out of forty, did I take it, answers. Four out of four double doses, stopped. Zero unsafe sentences. Pill matching found every known pill, and rejected every new one. Colour alone managed sixty two percent. Laya, without training, acted wrongly on one Sinhala question in four. So it stays off. Ammi keeps her big buttons. We would rather ship buttons, than a confident wrong answer.
s16: Open models. Open code. Running on an old phone, in a Sri Lankan home. Mathaka is not a medical device, and it does not replace a carer. It gives the family one less worry. A reminder is not remembering. Mathaka remembers.
